questions.q: What is the central philosophical claim D.H. Lawrence makes about the novel in "Why the Novel Matters"?
questions.a: The central claim is that the novel is the 'one bright book of life' and 'the book of life' because it alone can affect the *whole man alive* — body, mind, senses, contradictions — whereas philosophy, science, poetry, and religion only address fragmented parts (soul, mind, intellect, spirit). A wrong answer (e.g., 'the novel is the best form of entertainment' or 'the novel teaches moral lessons') reveals the student has confused Lawrence's *ontological* argument (about the nature of being alive) with a *functional* or *didactic* view of literature.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what Lawrence means by 'tremulations on the ether' and why he uses this metaphor for books and communication.
questions.a: 'Tremulations on the ether' refers to vibrations or waves transmitted through air/space — like radio signals — that are *not alive in themselves*. Lawrence uses it to show that all books, sermons, philosophical treatises, and scientific theories are merely dead vibrations until they reach a *living* human being who 'quivers' into new life. A wrong answer (e.g., 'it means books are magical' or 'it refers to the beauty of language') reveals the student has missed Lawrence's materialist point: communication is physically inert; only the *receiver's aliveness* gives it meaning.

questions.q: Lawrence writes: 'The whole is greater than the part. And therefore, I, who am man alive, am greater than my soul, or spirit, or body, or mind, or consciousness, or anything else that is merely a part of me.' Apply this logic to explain why he considers the novelist superior to the saint, the scientist, and the philosopher.
questions.a: The saint focuses on the soul, the scientist on the body/mechanism, the philosopher on the mind/intellect — each masters a *part* of the human being. The novelist, by portraying characters who *live* in their wholeness (contradictions, sensory details, flux), engages the *whole* person. Since the whole > any part, the novelist's domain (the whole man alive) is superior. A wrong answer (e.g., 'novelists are better writers' or 'novels are more popular') reveals the student hasn't grasped the *part-whole* ontology driving Lawrence's hierarchy.

questions.q: Analyse how Lawrence's biographical details (coal-mining background, miner father/teacher mother, itinerant life across continents) inform the essay's revolt against 'puritanism, mediocrity and the dehumanisation of an industrial society.'
questions.a: Lawrence's lived experience of the body-mind split (miner's physical labour vs. mother's intellectual ambition), the degradation of industrial labour, and the rootlessness of constant migration forged his conviction that *aliveness* resides in the integrated, sensing body — not in abstract ideals. The essay's defence of the 'hand' that 'flickers with a life of its own' against the 'mind that directs it' directly mirrors his parents' conflict. A wrong answer (e.g., 'he hated his father' or 'he travelled a lot') reduces biography to anecdote instead of tracing how *specific tensions* become *philosophical positions*.

questions.q: Evaluate Lawrence's rejection of 'absolutes' ('There is no absolute good, there is nothing absolutely right') in light of his claim that the novel helps us 'not to be dead man in life.' Is this a contradiction? Justify your answer.
questions.a: No contradiction. Lawrence rejects *fixed, external* absolutes (commandments, dogmas, scientific laws) that demand conformity and turn living people into 'dead man in life' (e.g., the 'good' man who becomes a corpse through rigid goodness). The novel's value is *processual*: it cultivates an *instinct for life* — a dynamic, bodily responsiveness to changing reality. The 'absolute' he rejects is static pattern; the 'guide' he offers is the novel's capacity to keep us alive *amid* flux. A wrong answer (e.g., 'yes it's a contradiction because he says novels are supreme') shows the student cannot distinguish between *static absolutism* and *dynamic vitality* as Lawrence defines them.

questions.q: Create a 3-sentence 'Before You Read' note for a classmate that captures the *one thing* they must grasp before reading the essay to avoid the most common misinterpretation.
questions.a: A strong answer: 'Lawrence isn't saying novels are "better" in a literary-ranking sense; he's saying the novel is the only form that mirrors the *wholeness* of a living human being — body, senses, contradictions, change — instead of slicing us into soul, mind, or body. Don't read it as literary criticism; read it as a philosophy of what it means to be alive. The key phrase is "man alive" — whenever you see it, substitute "a whole, sensing, contradictory human being."' A weak answer (e.g., 'Lawrence likes novels more than philosophy') reveals the student still sees this as preference/opinion rather than ontological argument.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: "Before You Read: Context and ______" prepares students to engage with D.H.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you're about to read an essay that claims a novel can do something philosophy, science, and religion cannot: make the *whole* human being — body, mind, senses, ______ — tremble with aliveness.
What is "Before You Read? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: "Before You Read: Context and Background" prepares students to engage with D.H.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain in their own words why Lawrence privileges the novel over philosophy, science, and poetry, and can identify the historical, biographical, and literary context that shapes the essay's argument about aliveness versus abstraction.
